migrationNotes: Spine: follow a glucose molecule into a cell, starting from a candle. The same reaction runs in small steps, the energy is caught in ATP and given off as heat, the carbon leaves as carbon dioxide, plants do it in the dark, and a sealed jar with a blank measures it.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): bio-fuel-to-cell-work-3 and -atoms-why. Whether a plant respires in the dark is taught on 'breathing-and-respiration' instead of being asked, and -atoms-why is covered by the 'following-the-carbon' screen.

lesson.title: How does a cell use its fuel?

lead.text: Cells run on the same sort of reaction as the candle, but they carry it out in a long chain of small steps, each one helped by an enzyme. Because each step releases only a little energy, the cell never overheats, and it can capture part of the energy at every stage. The set of reactions that transfers energy from a fuel such as glucose is called respiration. When it uses oxygen it is called aerobic respiration.

Written as an equation, aerobic respiration of glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ → 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O, with energy transferred. Put it beside the equation from the last lesson and it runs the other way. A leaf builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water, and a cell takes glucose apart again. Animal cells get their glucose from food. Plant cells make theirs, and light supplies the energy at the start of the loop.

afterFigure.text: The figure sets the two equations side by side. The atoms go round the loop, and the energy comes in as light and goes out as work and heat.

lead.text: The candle's wax left as carbon dioxide and water vapour. A cell's sugar leaves in much the same way.

A cell cannot spend glucose directly on its work. Instead, much of the energy released from glucose is used to build a small molecule called ATP, which works like a rechargeable battery. The mitochondria you met in the first lesson do most of this job. The cell then spends ATP wherever work is needed, such as moving parts of the cell, building new molecules and pushing substances across a membrane.
None of this is perfectly efficient. A good share of the energy cannot be captured in ATP and is given out as heat. That is why a crowded room warms up and why your body stays warm without a flame.
A cell uses up and rebuilds its ATP all the time. It is better to think of ATP as the way a cell carries energy to the place where it is needed than as a store of fuel.
A cell needs a way to carry energy from where sugar is taken apart to where work is done.

Next come the atoms. As in photosynthesis, atoms are rearranged in respiration and none are created or destroyed. The carbon atoms in glucose have to end up somewhere, and the equation shows where: all of them leave in carbon dioxide. Nothing is turned into energy. Energy is a separate matter, carried by ATP and given off as heat.

Every carbon atom ends up in exactly one CO₂ molecule, and a glucose holds six carbon atoms, so the count is simple. Three glucose molecules hold 3 × 6 = 18 carbon atoms, and breaking them down completely produces 18 CO₂ molecules. Count the carbon atoms in the fuel and you know how many CO₂ molecules are made.
Use the same counting for two glucose molecules.

People often use breathing and respiration as if they meant the same thing, and the difference matters. Breathing is the movement of air in and out of your lungs. It brings oxygen close to your blood and carries carbon dioxide away. Respiration is the chemistry inside your cells that uses that oxygen and the sugar. The two are linked, because breathing supplies what respiration needs, but one is a movement of air and the other a set of reactions.

A plant shows the difference clearly. It has no lungs and does not breathe, yet every one of its living cells respires. It makes glucose in the light and respires all the time, in the dark as well, because cells need ATP at every hour of the day. Light is needed to build the sugar and not to release its energy. Bacteria and mushrooms have no lungs either, and they respire too.
Both words come up whenever people talk about oxygen and carbon dioxide.

Respiration is hard to watch, but its effects can be measured. A living thing sealed in a jar uses up the oxygen as it respires, so the oxygen in the jar falls. Measure the amount at the start and again after a few minutes, and the difference is the oxygen the living thing used.

afterFigure.text: Careful experimenters also set up a blank, an identical jar with no living things in it. The blank shows what the apparatus does by itself, such as a little oxygen dissolving into water or a slight leak. In the figure the jar with organisms loses 6 units of oxygen in three minutes and the blank loses 1, so the organisms themselves used 6 − 1 = 5. Without the blank, the whole fall of 6 would be put down to the organisms.

lead.text: A sealed jar of living organisms loses oxygen as they respire.
Now the blank jar joins in. It is identical to the organism jar but holds no living things.

lesson.orientation: Connect respiration, ATP and conserved atoms without confusing breathing with cellular reactions.
lesson.reviewLabel: How does a cell use its fuel?
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A candle burns wax with oxygen from the air. The flame gives out heat and light, and the wax leaves as carbon dioxide and water vapour. Hold a cold glass over the flame and the water condenses on it as mist.

A cell does something very like this with sugar. It combines the sugar with oxygen, and the sugar leaves as carbon dioxide and water, just as the wax did. The energy stored in the sugar is released too. Yet a cell cannot flare up like a flame, because it would cook itself if all that energy came out as heat at once.

So the cell has to release the energy in small steps and catch it in a form it can spend. This lesson follows a molecule of sugar into a cell and finds where its atoms and its energy end up. At the close, a sealed jar shows how to measure the process.

intro.promise: By the end you'll say how a cell gets energy from sugar, follow its carbon atoms and tell breathing from what happens inside cells.

recap.keyIdea: Respiration transfers energy from fuel into ATP, and conserves the fuel's atoms in its products. Breathing is not the same thing.

blocks.text: A cell takes sugar apart in small steps, the way a candle burns wax in one go. The energy is caught in ATP or given off as heat, and every carbon atom of the sugar leaves in a molecule of carbon dioxide. Breathing only brings the oxygen in. You counted the CO₂ that a few glucose molecules produce, and you measured oxygen use in a sealed jar after taking off what the blank jar lost.

recap.nextHook: Respiration keeps a cell's work going, and the next lesson turns to a job a cell must do before it divides: copying a long message exactly, using two strips that zip together.

questions.prompt: Name the molecule that commonly transfers energy from respiration to cellular work.
hints: The name is three letters long.
It carries energy from where sugar is broken down to where work is done.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ATP couples energy-releasing processes to energy-requiring work.

questions.onCorrect: ATP. Cells fill it with energy from fuel, then spend it on work.

misconceptions.feedback: Glucose is the fuel. Name the molecule that carries the transferred energy to the work.

questions.prompt: A cell completely breaks down two glucose molecules using oxygen. How many CO₂ molecules does it produce?
hints: Each CO₂ contains one carbon.
Each glucose contains six carbons.
Count the carbon from two glucose molecules.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose contributes six carbon atoms: 2 × 6 = 12 CO₂.

questions.onCorrect: 12. Each carbon atom from the fuel ends up in one CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the CO₂ from one glucose. There are two.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms in them.

questions.prompt: A living plant has stored fuel and oxygen but no light. Name the energy-transfer process that can continue.
hints: Which process uses fuel rather than incoming light?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Respiration can use stored fuel in darkness even when photosynthesis stops.

questions.onCorrect: Respiration. It runs on stored fuel, so it carries on when the light goes.

misconceptions.feedback: Photosynthesis needs light, and there is none. Name the process that uses fuel.

questions.prompt: A sealed jar of living organisms holds 20 units of oxygen at the start and 11 units after three minutes. How many units were consumed?
hints: Compare the starting and final oxygen amounts.
The final amount is lower.
Subtract the final amount from the starting amount.
questions.onCorrect: 9 units. Falling oxygen in a sealed jar is a sign that organisms are respiring.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what was left. The question asks how much was used.
That adds the two amounts. Oxygen fell, so subtract.

questions.prompt: What happens to glucose's carbon when a cell breaks the glucose down completely using oxygen?
hints: Follow the carbon-containing substances.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Glucose carbon is conserved in CO₂; energy transfer does not destroy those atoms.

questions.onCorrect: It ends up in carbon dioxide. Atoms are conserved, and only the energy is transferred.

misconceptions.feedback: Matter doesn't turn into energy. The carbon atoms are still there afterwards.
Oxygen gas has no carbon in it. Look for a product that does.

questions.prompt: Which claim correctly separates breathing from cellular respiration?
hints: Compare moving air with chemistry in cells.

acceptedIdeas: Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Breathing can supply oxygen, but respiration is a set of chemical processes in cells.

choices.label: They are exactly the same reaction
Breathing moves air; cellular respiration transfers energy through chemical reactions

questions.onCorrect: Breathing moves air. Respiration is the chemistry that goes on in cells.

misconceptions.feedback: Breathing is a movement of air, not a reaction. Respiration is the reaction.
Plants and bacteria respire too, and they do not breathe.

questions.prompt: Not all the energy from fuel ends up in ATP. In what form does much of the rest disperse?
hints: Think about why your body is warm.
Energy that is not captured has to go somewhere.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Energy that is not transferred to ATP disperses as heat.

questions.onCorrect: Heat. Some energy always disperses as heat, which is why living things are warm.

misconceptions.feedback: Most cells give out very little light. Think about what a warm body gives off.

questions.prompt: A cell completely breaks down five glucose molecules using oxygen. How many carbon atoms end up in CO₂?
hints: How many carbon atoms does one glucose have?
All the carbon from the fuel ends up in CO₂.
Multiply the carbon atoms in one glucose by five.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each glucose has six carbon atoms, and all of them end up in CO₂: 5 × 6 = 30.

questions.onCorrect: 30. Carbon is conserved, so every carbon atom in the fuel ends up in CO₂.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the carbon in one glucose. There are five.
That counts the glucose molecules. Count the carbon atoms in them.

questions.prompt: Which gas, made when cells use sugar as fuel, do you breathe out?
hints: Look at the right-hand side of the equation.
It is also what a candle gives out.
Its formula is CO₂.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cells release carbon dioxide when they use sugar as fuel.

questions.onCorrect: Carbon dioxide. Cells use sugar and oxygen, and carbon dioxide is one of the products.

misconceptions.feedback: Oxygen is what the cells use up. Name the gas they give out.

questions.prompt: Why can you count the CO₂ by counting the carbon atoms in the fuel?
hints: Think about what happens to atoms in any chemical reaction.

acceptedIdeas: Carbon atoms are rearranged into the products, not destroyed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Atoms are conserved, so the carbon from the fuel ends up in the products.

choices.label: Carbon atoms are rearranged into the products, not destroyed
Carbon atoms are turned into energy

questions.onCorrect: Atoms are conserved. The carbon is rearranged into CO₂, so the counts match.

misconceptions.feedback: Energy and atoms are different things. Atoms are never turned into energy in a cell.
Oxygen is a reactant here, but the carbon comes from the fuel.

questions.prompt: A blank jar with no organisms also loses 2 units of oxygen in the same three minutes, while the organism jar loses 9. How many units did the organisms themselves use?
hints: Some oxygen is lost even without organisms.
The blank shows the loss that is not the organisms' doing.
Take the blank's loss off the organisms' jar.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 9 − 2 = 7 units. The blank's loss is not the organisms' doing.

questions.onCorrect: 7 units. The blank shows the loss due to the apparatus, so subtract it to isolate the organisms.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the organism jar's total loss. Part of it also happens in the blank.
That adds the two losses. The blank's loss should come off.
